version_history.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: fix double release of data space on failed direct IO COW write

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a double release of data space on failed direct IO copy-on-write (COW) writes in the Btrfs file system. The issue occurs when a COW write fails after reserving data space, causing the reserved extent to be freed and then releasing all allocated data space again. This results in an underflow of available data space, leading to warnings and clamping to zero. The patch records the consumed length during reservation and releases only the remaining allocated data space on error, preventing the double release and fixing the issue.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new NUMA hinting scan mode called 'promotion-only' that allows the kernel to focus on identifying when VMAs become active, rather than optimizing scanning activity based on heuristics like read-only VMAs or VMA activeness. The patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY and modifies various functions in the mm module to use this flag to determine the type of walk to perform. This change is necessary for memory-tiering fixes and improves the interface by keeping it focused on scan intent, rather than plumbing VMA-derived state.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from slow memory to a faster tier, while maintaining existing restrictions for ordinary placement and non-promotion migrations. The patch renames the `folio_use_access_time` function to `folio_numab_promotable` to better reflect its purpose in handling memory-tiering and source-tier tests. This change enables promotion of low-tier folios to top-tier memory, but prevents east-west or north-to-south migrations. The patch addresses an issue with NUMA balancing that previously rejected shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios from being promoted.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only performs promotion scans on these mappings. This change prevents hot file folios from being placed on slow memory in tiering mode, which can cause east-west placement bouncing. The patch also updates the walk type for each VMA (Virtual Memory Area) based on the balancing-mode snapshot taken in task_numa_work().

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the logic of VMA placement from scan continuation in the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) scheduling code. The existing `vma_is_accessed` function returns true for both placement eligibility and scan progress, which is not distinguishable by callers. This patch renames the function to `vma_needs_placement_scan`, introduces a new field in the `struct vma_numab_state` to track promotion-only scans, and updates the task's NUMA work to handle continuation state correctly. The separation allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned for promotion without treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series enhances the vma scanning logic in the Linux kernel's scheduler to promote hot slow-tier memory by bypassing a filter that skips VMAs without recent PID activity. The patch introduces a new sequence ID for placement scans and updates the starvation horizon calculation to prevent promotion-only scans from postponing placement indefinitely.

on source=nodes.

> ---

Thanks, this is a fair point. Sorry, I also made that earlier
explanation too long, so let me summarize the intended use cases here:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/67fcd8db-269d-43f1-aea2-8c41165747d0@bytedance.com/

In short, performance, fairness and cost are all part of the goal. One
target is mixed DRAM/CXL systems where user space keeps each memcg near
its own DRAM/CXL resident ratio target, based on the workload's
latency/throughput and cost requirements. Another target is the case you
described below, where user space wants memcg-scoped reclaim to apply
pressure to the desired tier first, rather than reclaiming from warmer
memory on the top tier. This is especially useful when a memcg is close
to its memory limit and user space wants charge-reducing reclaim to
start from colder/lower-tier memory first.

> I CAN see why you might want to proactively shape what data is swapped.
> Let me give you an example:
> 
> ---
> The global node reclaim interfaces allow us to put pressure on distinct
> nodes - which lets us shape which node is swapped from first.
> 
> Example: node0-1=DRAM, node2-3:CXL
> 
>   echo 1G > node2/reclaim   # swap from CXL
>   echo 1G > node3/reclaim   # swap from CXL
>   echo 1G > node0/reclaim   # demote to CXL
>   echo 1G > node1/reclaim   # demote to CXL
> 
> But the memcg.reclaim interface only allows us to pressure the complete
> set of cpuset.mems nodes for that memcg
> 
>   cat cpuset.mems           # 0-3
>   echo 1G > memory.reclaim  # makes progress from any of 0-3
> 
> Presently, proactive reclaim iterates nodes in node or fallback order,
> meaning it attempts to make progress from the fastest node possible
> first - which attempts to demote by default.  If the lower nodes are
> full, this demotion will fail and we'll swap directly from the top tier,
> which is (presumably) warmer than the bottom tiers.
> 
> Enable source-bound reclaim in the memory.reclaim interface so that user
> space can have the same control over memcg memory tiers that global
> proactive reclaim has.
> 
>   echo 2G source=nodes:2-3 > memory.reclaim  # [z]swap from CXL
>   echo 2G source=nodes:0-1 > memory.reclaim  # demote to CXL
> 
> This lets user proactive reclaim to target the coldest memory first
> rather than preferring to reclaim from node0 first and potentially
> swap out memory warmer than what is present on a CXL tier.
> ---
> 
> With this, you might be able to demonstrate fewer refaults and less
> DRAM (node0) memory consumed by zswap. These are clear benefits.

Thanks for the example. It makes the problem much easier to discuss. I
will refer to it when reworking the v3 motivation, and will avoid
framing the issue as a generic flexibility problem.

review_comments.raw_body:
On 11/13/26 1:04 AM, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> On 2026-11-11 12:55 -0500, Tal Zussman wrote:
>> migrate_vma_setup() installs a migration entry for each page it
>> collects, which carries the uffd bit over to the new PTE. However, a PTE
>> that maps the zero page is left in place without a migration entry.
>> migrate_vma_insert_page() later overwrites it with a new PTE that is
>> built only from the VMA flags, so the uffd-wp bit or the RWP PAGE_NONE
>> protection of the old PTE is lost. The same applies to the huge zero
>> PMD.
>> 
>> Once a driver has migrated such a zero page, writes and accesses to it
>> no longer fault into userfaultfd, so the manager misses them. With async
>> tracking, PAGEMAP_SCAN unconditionally reports the page as written or
>> accessed.
>> 
>> This requires a driver that migrates memory to a device.
>> 
>> To fix it, do not mark a zero page for migration if its entry has the
>> uffd bit set in a VMA registered for WP or RWP. The driver sees an
>> address that was not migrated, which drivers already have to deal with.
>> 
>> The uffd bit can also be set after the zero page was collected, as
>> write-protecting only takes the mmap lock for read. So check again under
>> the page table lock in migrate_vma_insert_page() and
>> migrate_vma_insert_huge_pmd_page().
>> 
> 
> Similar to last patch, this changelog could be improved.  My best
> attempt at summarizing:
> 
> """
> Device migration replaces a zero-page mapping with a fresh entry,
> losing its userfaultfd WP or RWP protection.
> 
> Don't migrate the uffd-protected zero pages.
> 
> Skip protected zero pages during collection. Check again under the
> page-table lock before insertion, because another thread can apply
> protection after collection finishes.
> 
> The alternative ...
> """
> 

Thanks, I'll trim it along these lines.

> I have concerns with this:
> 
>> The alternative would be to carry the uffd state over in
>> migrate_vma_insert_page() and migrate_vma_insert_huge_pmd_page(). Not
>> migrating the zero page is simpler, and a zero page that is protected by
>> userfaultfd in a range that a driver migrates should be rare.
> 
> This basically force-fails a migration of a uffd protected zero page.
> 
> Wouldn't we expect this to cause drivers to fail to make progress if
> they require that page to be resident on the device?  Not sure we want
> to force drivers to try to handle this special case (if they even can).
> 
> We'll need some input from the migrate_device/GPU folks.
> 

Yeah, makes sense. I can implement the alternative approach, but testing
for this is a little tricky without the right devices... I might drop this
patch and send it separately with the GPU folks on Cc.

> -- 
> ~Gregory
>

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1] mm/rmap: fix migration entries being treated as partial unmaps

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where migration entries in the Linux kernel are being treated as partial unmaps, leading to incorrect behavior such as unnecessary folio splits and overcounting of split_deferred statistics. The problem occurs when a large anonymous folio is migrated or split, causing the PG_partially_mapped flag to be set even though no actual unmapping has taken place. To fix this, the patch introduces a new flag that prevents __folio_remove_rmap() from marking a folio as partially mapped when migration entries are replaced for PTEs. This ensures that only actual unmappings trigger the deferred split queue and corrects the statistics. The patch also addresses issues related to migrated folios being queued for unnecessary splits and overcounting of split_deferred statistics.

commit 354dffd29575cdf13154e8fb787322354aa9efc4
Author: Barry Song <baohua@kernel.org>
Date:   Fri Feb 14 22:30:14 2025 +1300

    mm: support batched unmap for lazyfree large folios during reclamation

    Currently, the PTEs and rmap of a large folio are removed one at a time.
    This is not only slow but also causes the large folio to be unnecessarily
    added to deferred_split, which can lead to races between the
    deferred_split shrinker callback and memory reclamation.  This patch
    releases all PTEs and rmap entries in a batch.  Currently, it only handles
    lazyfree large folios.

Batching resolves the problem in the common case. For the remaining parts, we
should likely just check in the deferred split handler whether actually
partially mapped to then clear the flag if not.

Cheers,

David

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 1/7] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths. This makes it easier to follow the code, especially when page_counter_try_charge is made stock-aware. The change does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 2/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation for the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing implementation in memcg. The new struct page_counter_stock_pcp preserves the functionality of its memcg equivalent and adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. It also includes functions for draining, refilling, and flushing the counter, which are currently disconnected but will be connected later in the series. This patch does not introduce any functional changes and is intended as a preparatory step for further modifications.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 3/7] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge function to be stock-aware, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. It introduces two new parameters: may_batch and nr_charged. The may_batch parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios, where the goal is to charge as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The nr_charged parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving existing batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high. This patch preserves existing accounting heuristics and does not introduce any functional changes since no page_counter has stock yet.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 4/7] mm/memcontrol: check PF_MEMALLOC after trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the handling of PF_MEMALLOC charges in the Linux kernel's memory control code. It checks for PF_MEMALLOC after trying to consume stock, rather than before, and forces a charge if it fails or hits a limit. This change is necessary because a later patch moves the memory stock into the page counter, leaving no room between consuming stock and trying limits for the PF_MEMALLOC check.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 5/7] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient and accurate tracking of memory usage. It addresses issues with uncharge paths and divergent charges between memory and swap counters. The patch also preserves legacy behaviors such as equal-limit no-swap behavior and introduces new logic to prevent reclaiming when memory fails first. The changes are intended to pave the way for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking existing functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 6/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a stock to the memsw page counter in the Linux kernel's memory control module (mm/memcontrol.c). The new stock allows for independent handling of memory and swap counters, enabling them to be charged, refilled, drained, and hotplugged separately. This change also introduces a common drain scheduling function, schedule_stock_drain(), which is used by both stocks. series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new page flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows folios to be freed only after an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. This is done to prevent CPUs from bouncing the reference count of a page cache folio while it's being read by multiple processes. This patch also introduces a new counter in /proc/vmstat to track the number of deferred pages.

review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that making PG_rcu_free specific to one special freeing path would make the code fragile, less obvious, and limit its potential usefulness and applicability across the kernel.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think you're making things worse rather than better.

The whole point was to hook into *one* place: the page freeing.

Trying to make it specific to one special freeing path only makes it
fragile and less obvious, and results in anybody who then uses some
other freeing model to miss the RCU thing.

It also means that suddenly nobody else can use the RCU path for their own uses.

Look at all the kmalloc RCU freeing: it's used all over the place. RCU
has basically taken over the kernel. Every single performance-critical
lock-free area of the kernel wants RCU freeing.

I think trying to corral it into some special case is the last thing
we want to do. It only makes things less potentially useful and more
fragile.

review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Linus Torvalds pointed out that RCU freeing of pages is already implemented in other areas, such as TLB shootdown, and suggested that the new PG_rcu_free flag could have been designed to be more straightforward if it had been introduced earlier. He noted that existing hacks in this area are complicated due to the complexity of architecture-specific code and would be painful to convert to a new order.
review_comments.raw_body:
So for an example of a place that already does RCU freeing of pages -
*not* folios - look at the TLB shootdown.

It's very round-about and hard to tell, but it's using

  tlb_remove_table_free
    call_rcu(&batch->rcu, tlb_remove_table_rcu);

and that then does

  tlb_remove_table_rcu ->
    __tlb_remove_table_free ->
      __tlb_remove_table ->
        pagetable_dtor_free ->
          pagetable_free ->
            __pagetable_free ->
               __free_pages(page, compound_order(page))

(and I might have messed this up - this really is a rats nest of
nested inline functions).

And in order to do this all, it sets up *another* page just to contain
the batching (which is also RCU-free'd)

Now, the batching is probably a very good thing in that context, so
I'm not actually suggesting this should be converted to some common
RCU-freeing thing.

Rather, I'm pointing out that we have existing hacks in this area that
have grown up over time and would have been a *lot* less hacky if we
had had a proper RCU-freeing page allocator back when that whole TLB
freeing code was written.

So I'm not saying "we should unify this". But I *am* saying "look, RCU
freeing of pages is _already_ a thing, and we have complicated hacky
things in place for it".

And they are complicated not because they necessarily should be
complicated, but because we solved the TLB shootdown after we already
had tons of complex architecture-specific code in place, and we
basically ended up adding that RCU phase on top of that existing
per-architecture complexity and abstraction.

*NOW* it would be actually fairly painful to try to convert the TLB
shootdown to a new order. But originally, it would have been very nice
if we had just had a "Oh, mark this page for RCU freeing".

(In all fairness, we also did it that way because some architectures
don't need the RCU delay simply because they have some other hardware
page walking infrastructure than the actual page tables the kernel
builds up. Not that those architectures *matter* today, but some of
that per-architecture inline function stuff is required to basically
isolate these kinds of decisions from the MM code - that deep inline
function indirection has a reason that is entirely independent of the
freeing side).

                    Linus

purposes by some architectures) and some things about multiple page tables
residing in a single physical page on some architectures (at least powerpc),

There are some dirty details when it comes to the upcoming page vs. folio split
that I am still unclear about.

The page table example you mention above is another prime example of the

("ptdesc"), just like folios will have their memdesc ("folio") separately allocated.

When RCU freeing, we'll really have to keep the allocated memdesc alive as well.

And freeing memdescs through RCU will likely be memdesc specific.

I really don't know, Willy might know more about these plans.

But I am overloaded with all the Fixes, so my brain doesn't work quite right.

Cheers,

David

series_items.patch_summary: This patch aims to improve the performance of deferred frees in the Linux kernel by introducing an expedited grace period when a CPU has many pending folios (memory allocations). When more than 4 MiB is pending on a CPU, the patch takes both lists and frees them after an expedited grace period. The goal is to prevent memory bottlenecks and improve system responsiveness, especially during bulk frees triggered by operations like file truncation or fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED).

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 06/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before OOM
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to free pages waiting for a grace period before invoking the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer. When reclaim fails, it checks if freeing these waiting pages and what reclaim can still free would bring an eligible zone above its minimum watermark. If so, it drains these pages straight to the buddy lists, allowing the OOM killer to be invoked only when necessary. This approach is designed to reduce the likelihood of invoking the OOM killer unnecessarily, which can lead to system instability.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 07/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before isolation fails
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where migration of pages to a new zone fails due to pages waiting for a grace period after being freed. The patch introduces a new function, `rcu_free_sync()`, which frees all waiting folios and their associated work. This allows the allocation process to proceed without failing due to pending page migrations. The change is made in two key functions: `offline_pages()` and `alloc_contig_range()`. In `offline_pages()`, if a migration pass has occurred and there are pages waiting for a grace period, the function calls `rcu_free_sync()` before retrying the allocation. Similarly, in `alloc_contig_range()`, if the check for isolated pages fails due to pending migrations, the function frees any waiting folios before attempting to allocate memory again.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 08/18] mm/compaction: free the migrated folios that wait for a grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the Linux kernel's compaction mechanism, where migrated folios that wait for a grace period can cause compaction to fail more often. The problem arises when a block is migrated and its folios are not immediately freed, causing subsequent migrations to occur unnecessarily. To resolve this, the patch introduces a new function `rcu_free_drain()` that frees these waiting folios before draining the per-cpu lists. This change improves compaction efficiency and reduces allocation stalls in defrag_mode.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 09/18] mm/memory-failure: handle folios with PG_rcu_free
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where memory_failure() and soft_offline_page() cannot handle pages that are waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy-Update) grace period, which causes them to be ignored or handled incorrectly. The patch introduces a new function mf_free_rcu_pages() that frees these pages before attempting to access them, ensuring they are properly handled by memory_failure(). Additionally, it modifies the get_any_page() and memory_failure() functions to wait for an RCU grace period after setting PG_hwpoison on a page, allowing readers to safely unmap the poisoned page. This patch aims to improve the handling of pages waiting for an RCU grace period in the Linux kernel's memory failure mechanism.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 10/18] mm: have folio_mark_accessed() return whether the folio is hot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `folio_mark_accessed` function to return a boolean value indicating whether the accessed folio is considered 'hot'. A hot folio is one that is either unevictable or has its access flags set. This change prepares for reading the status of folios without requiring an explicit reference to them. The patch updates the `folio_mark_accessed` function and related code in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 11/18] mm/filemap: mark a folio accessed in one place in filemap_read()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the filemap_read() function by moving the folio access marking into a single helper function, filemap_read_accessed(). This function is called once per folio in the loop, eliminating duplicate code and making it easier to decide which folios are worth reading without a reference. The change does not affect the behavior of the function, but prepares for future improvements.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 12/18] mm/filemap: set PG_rcu_free on the folios that reads keep coming back to
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows the kernel to delay freeing memory associated with a folio that is frequently accessed by readers. The flag is set in filemap_read() when a folio is found to be hot based on LRU records or previous read access patterns. This approach aims to balance the trade-off between delaying free of streaming reads and truncating files, while also avoiding unnecessary delays for cold data. The patch includes changes to various kernel files to support this new flag and provide statistics on its usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 13/18] mm/filemap: read from the page cache without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the page cache read performance by allowing reads to occur without taking a reference on the folio, reducing the bounce of refcounts between CPUs. It achieves this by copying data from folios that are about to be freed under RCU read lock and using a batch size of up to 512 KiB per section. The patch also optimizes large folios and introduces checks for poisoned pages, uptodate status, and other conditions that require the slow path. This approach aims to reduce overhead and improve performance in scenarios with multiple CPUs accessing the same file.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 14/18] mm/filemap: read large folios without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's filemap module to allow reading large folios without creating a reference to them. A large folio is one that spans all or none of its range, and once the last page in its range is reached, subsequent pages can be copied from the same folio. The patch introduces a new function `filemap_read_rcu_size` to calculate how much data can be copied from a folio without creating a reference. It also updates the `filemap_read_rcu_lookup` function to handle large folios and split them correctly when necessary. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of references created during file I/O operations.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 15/18] mm/filemap: don't store f_ra.prev_pos for FMODE_RANDOM files
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the filemap_read function to skip storing f_ra.prev_pos for files that have FMODE_RANDOM set, which is used by applications like RocksDB to read files at random offsets from multiple threads. The patch addresses a performance issue where reads were slower due to unnecessary shared store operations. It keeps the slow path of the function intact and only skips the store operation when filemap_read_rcu has already done a full read without folio references.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 16/18] mm/shmem: count accesses to a folio the way filemap_read() does
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way accesses to a folio in tmpfs are counted. Instead of only marking a folio as accessed when a read starts at its beginning, it marks the folio accessed unless the previous read through the file ended in the same position. This change ensures that reads that start anywhere within a folio count towards its access age, rather than just those that start at the beginning. Additionally, this patch sets PG_rcu_free on tmpfs folios that are repeatedly accessed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 17/18] mm/shmem: read without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the shmem_file_read_iter function to take a reference on every folio it reads, which can cause small reads of one tmpfs file from many CPUs to bounce the folio's refcount. To fix this issue, the patch introduces a new function called filemap_read_rcu that copies data from the page cache without taking any references. This function is used in place of shmem_file_read_iter for small reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same tmpfs file simultaneously without causing reference count bounces.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 18/18] mm/filemap: add a debugfs switch for lockless page cache reads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a debugfs switch to control lockless page cache reads in the Linux kernel. The goal is to provide a way to turn off lockless reads, which can be problematic for certain workloads or when there's a bug in the read path. The switch is added as a static key that can be enabled or disabled through debugfs. When enabled, it stops filemap_read() and shmem_file_read_iter() from setting PG_rcu_free and copying without a reference. This allows users to test and verify the correctness of lockless reads before they are enabled by default.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series proposes a change to how Linux handles page cache reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same folio without taking a reference. This is done by introducing a new flag PG_rcu_free and deferring the freeing of folios until an RCU grace period. The goal is to reduce contention between readers and improve performance in scenarios where many threads are reading the same pages. The patch series includes 18 patches that implement this change, including modifications to filemap_read(), shmem, and other related functions.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Reading a page cache folio without taking a reference would keep CPUs
that read the same file from bouncing its refcount.  But without a
reference the folio can be freed, and its memory reused, while the
reader copies from it.

Add PG_rcu_free: the free of a folio with the flag waits for an RCU
grace period.  A reader that saw the flag under rcu_read_lock(), and
then still found the folio where it looked, can read it until
rcu_read_unlock().  A split copies the flag, as such a reader may still
be reading the new folios.

The folios wait on per-CPU lists, one grace period in flight per CPU:
call_rcu() per folio would queue a callback for every folio of a
truncated file.  A work, which can reschedule, frees each batch.
Reclaim depends on these frees, so the workqueue is WQ_MEM_RECLAIM.

The flag is 64-bit only (CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE): page flags are scarce
on 32-bit, and the contention this avoids is a problem of large
machines.  It is off on PREEMPT_RT, where expedited grace periods are
normal ones, so the waiting pages cannot be freed quickly when memory
runs short.

pgfree_rcu in /proc/vmstat counts the deferred pages.  Nothing sets the
flag yet.

+/*
+ * Each CPU has at most one grace period in flight (@queued), covering
+ * @batch.  Folios freed meanwhile wait on @pending for the next one.
+ */
+struct rcu_free_pcpu {
+	spinlock_t lock;
+	bool queued;
+	struct list_head pending;
+	struct list_head batch;
+	struct rcu_work rwork;
+};
+
+static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct rcu_free_pcpu, rcu_free_pcpu);
+
+static struct workqueue_struct *rcu_free_wq __ro_after_init;
+
+static void rcu_free_start(struct rcu_free_pcpu *r)
+{
+	lockdep_assert_held(&r->lock);
+
+	if (r->queued || list_empty(&r->pending))
+		return;
+
+	list_splice_init(&r->pending, &r->batch);
+	r->queued = true;
+	WARN_ON_ONCE(!queue_rcu_work(rcu_free_wq, &r->rwork));
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_pages(struct list_head *list)
+{
+	struct folio_batch fbatch;
+	struct folio *folio, *next;
+
+	folio_batch_init(&fbatch);
+	list_for_each_entry_safe(folio, next, list, lru) {
+		if (!folio_batch_add(&fbatch, folio)) {
+			free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+			cond_resched_tasks_rcu_qs();
+		}
+	}
+	if (folio_batch_count(&fbatch))
+		free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_workfn(struct work_struct *work)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = container_of(to_rcu_work(work),
+					       struct rcu_free_pcpu, rwork);
+	LIST_HEAD(done);
+
+	spin_lock_irq(&r->lock);
+	list_splice_init(&r->batch, &done);
+	r->queued = false;
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irq(&r->lock);
+
+	rcu_free_pages(&done);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_defer(struct folio *folio)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = raw_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu);
+	unsigned long flags;
+
+	spin_lock_irqsave(&r->lock, flags);
+	list_add_tail(&folio->lru, &r->pending);
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irqrestore(&r->lock, flags);
+}
+
+static void __init rcu_free_init(void)
+{
+	int cpu;
+
+	if (!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE))
+		return;
+
+	rcu_free_wq = alloc_workqueue("rcu_free",
+				      WQ_MEM_RECLAIM | WQ_PERCPU, 0);
+
+	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu) {
+		struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = per_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu, cpu);
+
+		spin_lock_init(&r->lock);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->pending);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->batch);
+		INIT_RCU_WORK(&r->rwork, rcu_free_workfn);
+	}
+}

PG_rcu_free holds back the reuse of a folio's memory until a grace
period after the folio is freed.  A stolen page cache pipe buffer is
reused without being freed: remove_mapping() takes the folio out of the

a fuse file, where writes change it under a reader that found it before
the steal.

and virtio_console's pipe_to_sg() then copy, as they already do when
stealing fails.  SPLICE_F_MOVE from the page cache into a fuse file or
a virtio console now copies.

fuse_try_move_folio() takes the folio of a pipe buffer and puts it into
a fuse file, where writes change it.  A folio with PG_rcu_free may still
be copied by a lockless page cache read that found it before it left
the page cache.

vmsplice(SPLICE_F_GIFT) and its file is then truncated.
fuse_check_folio() refuses it only because the flag is not among those

review_comments.raw_body:
A page whose free waits for an RCU grace period has refcount 0 and is
neither on the LRU nor in the buddy allocator.  memory_failure() and
soft_offline_page() cannot handle such a page: get_any_page() retries a
few times and gives up.  Soft offline of the page fails, and a hard
error is ignored.  If the page is part of a large folio, the folio is
later freed with the poisoned page in it, and that page can be handed
out again.

Free the waiting pages first when the page looks like one of them, and
again on each retry in get_any_page(): the page can be freed while it
retries.  memory_failure() has to do it before it sets PG_hwpoison.  The
free of a poisoned order-0 page drops the page instead of returning it
to the buddy allocator, so a later drain would still leave the error
ignored.

A folio with PG_rcu_free that is still in use may be copied by a reader
that holds no reference.  When memory_failure() succeeds, its caller can
unmap the page from the direct map under such a reader.  Wait for a
grace period before returning success.  By then the page has left the
page cache, or is an order-0 folio with PG_hwpoison, which a reader that
starts after the grace period has to check.

Wait at the end, not right after setting PG_hwpoison.  A large folio is
split later, and until the new folios are in the page cache, a reader
can still copy the poisoned page as part of the large one.

Both callers hold mf_mutex and can wait for the grace period.

+	if (page_count(p))

>

> doing this in a folio-specific helper?

I think you're making things worse rather than better.

The whole point was to hook into *one* place: the page freeing.

Trying to make it specific to one special freeing path only makes it
fragile and less obvious, and results in anybody who then uses some
other freeing model to miss the RCU thing.

It also means that suddenly nobody else can use the RCU path for their own uses.

Look at all the kmalloc RCU freeing: it's used all over the place. RCU
has basically taken over the kernel. Every single performance-critical
lock-free area of the kernel wants RCU freeing.

I think trying to corral it into some special case is the last thing
we want to do. It only makes things less potentially useful and more
fragile.

> > we want to do. It only makes things less potentially useful and more
> > fragile.
> Let me wrap my head around how this would look when we decouple pages from
> folios, where pages might not have a ->lru anymore, or not even a refcount.

So for an example of a place that already does RCU freeing of pages -
*not* folios - look at the TLB shootdown.

It's very round-about and hard to tell, but it's using

  tlb_remove_table_free
    call_rcu(&batch->rcu, tlb_remove_table_rcu);

and that then does

  tlb_remove_table_rcu ->
    __tlb_remove_table_free ->
      __tlb_remove_table ->
        pagetable_dtor_free ->
          pagetable_free ->
            __pagetable_free ->
               __free_pages(page, compound_order(page))

(and I might have messed this up - this really is a rats nest of
nested inline functions).

And in order to do this all, it sets up *another* page just to contain
the batching (which is also RCU-free'd)

Now, the batching is probably a very good thing in that context, so
I'm not actually suggesting this should be converted to some common
RCU-freeing thing.

Rather, I'm pointing out that we have existing hacks in this area that
have grown up over time and would have been a *lot* less hacky if we
had had a proper RCU-freeing page allocator back when that whole TLB
freeing code was written.

So I'm not saying "we should unify this". But I *am* saying "look, RCU
freeing of pages is _already_ a thing, and we have complicated hacky
things in place for it".

And they are complicated not because they necessarily should be
complicated, but because we solved the TLB shootdown after we already
had tons of complex architecture-specific code in place, and we
basically ended up adding that RCU phase on top of that existing
per-architecture complexity and abstraction.

*NOW* it would be actually fairly painful to try to convert the TLB
shootdown to a new order. But originally, it would have been very nice
if we had just had a "Oh, mark this page for RCU freeing".

builds up. Not that those architectures *matter* today, but some of
that per-architecture inline function stuff is required to basically
isolate these kinds of decisions from the MM code - that deep inline
function indirection has a reason that is entirely independent of the
freeing side).

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page allocation watermark check in the Linux kernel to take into account the migratetype of the request. series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation system to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag. When this flag is set, the check should not consider free pages from other migration types when determining whether an allocation can be made. This change aims to prevent unnecessary stalls in compaction and improve performance under memory pressure. The patch also updates the __compact_finished function to follow the same rule for its fallback test. As a result, allocations that may not wake kswapd or reclaim will fall back to smaller folios instead of stalling in compaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag from the allocation down to try_to_free_pages(). This allows the allocation to take free pages of any migratetype, rather than being limited to unmovable and reclaimable pageblocks. The change is intended to improve performance by reducing fragmentation during direct reclaim. The patch was tested on a 64K mTHP benchmark and showed improved results with defrag_mode enabled.
